name: Thioridazine (Mellaril)
summary: Older (first-generation) antipsychotic reserved for schizophrenia when other antipsychotics don’t work or aren’t tolerated. Effective for psychosis but carries a serious, dose-related QTc prolongation risk that can lead to dangerous arrhythmias and sudden death.
description: Thioridazine is a first-generation antipsychotic sometimes used for schizophrenia when other options fail. It can reduce hallucinations, delusions, agitation, and disorganization over weeks, but it’s not a go-to medication today because it can dangerously prolong the QTc interval (risk of torsades de pointes and sudden death). It can also cause sedation, anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision), orthostatic hypotension, movement side effects (EPS), tardive dyskinesia, and rare blood count problems. It’s not approved for dementia-related psychosis and can raise mortality risk in that population.
patient_summary: Thioridazine is an older antipsychotic used for schizophrenia only when other antipsychotics haven’t worked or weren’t tolerable. It can help psychosis and agitation, but it has a real, dose-related risk of QTc prolongation that can cause life-threatening heart rhythm problems. If you’re on it, you need careful ECG monitoring, avoidance of QT-prolonging meds, and a plan with psychiatry to use the lowest effective dose.

primary_indications: Schizophrenia (reserved use when other antipsychotics are ineffective or not tolerated)

linked_conditions.context: Reserved option for schizophrenia when at least two adequate antipsychotic trials have failed due to poor efficacy or intolerable adverse effects.
May reduce psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganization), but safety limitations make it an uncommon choice.
Can be sedating and may reduce agitation in schizophrenia, but QTc risk and side effects limit its role.

contraindications: Concurrent use with other QTc-prolonging medications
Concurrent use with CYP2D6 inhibitors (including fluoxetine, paroxetine) or fluvoxamine
Concurrent use with propranolol or pindolol
Known genetic defect causing reduced CYP2D6 activity (poor metabolizer status)
Severe hyper- or hypotensive heart disease

efficacy_response.metric: Time to meaningful improvement in psychosis
efficacy_response.patient_text: Thioridazine can help psychosis, but the main clinical issue isn’t whether it works—it’s that its cardiac risk profile forces it into a last-line role.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: FDA Label + APA Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidance

pharmacokinetics.onset: Schizophrenia: early effects often noticed in 1-2 weeks, with continued improvement through 4-6 weeks
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic (multiple pathways). Major CYP2D6 involvement with active metabolites (mesoridazine, sulforidazine)

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Thioridazine is a last-line antipsychotic for schizophrenia. It’s reserved for people who didn’t get an acceptable response to other antipsychotics, either because those meds didn’t work well enough or because side effects made it impossible to reach an effective dose. The reason it’s “reserved” is simple: it can prolong the QTc in a dose-related way and has been linked to torsades de pointes–type arrhythmias and sudden death.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia}: Reserved treatment when other antipsychotics have been inadequate or not tolerated

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s brain chemistry is different, but here’s the kind of “day-to-day feel” people often describe with thioridazine:

quotes: My thoughts weren’t as loud. Everything felt less intense.
The edge came off. I wasn’t spiraling as hard.
I felt more steady, like I wasn’t constantly on high alert.
It helped, but I was sleepy… like my brain was wrapped in a blanket.
I could finally sit still, but I also felt kind of slow.
It knocked down the agitation, but I needed more sleep.
items.note: Sedation can be strong early on and during dose increases.

quotes: Dry mouth was real. I was carrying water everywhere.
Constipation was the annoying part nobody warned me about enough.
My vision got blurry sometimes, especially at night.
items.note: Thioridazine is known for relatively strong anticholinergic effects compared to many other antipsychotics.

quotes: If I stood up too fast, I’d get that head-rush feeling.
I had to move slower or I’d feel lightheaded.
Stairs were sketchy for a while.
items.note: This can increase fall risk, especially in older adults.

quotes: I didn’t love needing ECGs, but I liked knowing we were watching it.
The QT thing made me cautious about other meds and supplements.
I felt better once we had a clear plan for monitoring.
items.note: This medication requires serious attention to QTc risk and drug interactions.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Thioridazine isn’t an instant switch. Some people notice early changes within a week or two, but the bigger gains in psychosis and functional stability typically build over several weeks.
key_points: 1-2 weeks: Early changes may show up (less agitation, less intensity of psychosis for some people)
4-6 weeks: More meaningful and sustained symptom improvement is more likely to be clear
1-4 hours: Time to peak blood levels after a dose (not the same as full psychiatric benefit)
5-27 hours: Highly variable half-life (how long it sticks around depends on the person)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Thioridazine can reduce psychotic symptoms, but modern practice treats it as an alternative agent, not a first- or second-line choice. The limiting factor is safety—especially its dose-related QTc prolongation and risk of torsades de pointes and sudden death. In real-life decision-making, “Does it work?” is usually followed immediately by “Is it safe enough for this specific patient?”
sections.clinical_details: When thioridazine is used, clinicians typically aim for the lowest effective maintenance dose and reassess frequently. Response is often judged by reductions in hallucinations/delusions, improved organization, reduced agitation, better sleep continuity, and improved functioning over weeks. The medication’s anticholinergic and sedating profile may make it feel calming, but those same properties can impair cognition, contribute to constipation/urinary retention, and increase fall risk.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Dose-related QTc prolongation can cause torsades de pointes and sudden death. This is why thioridazine is reserved for last-line use in schizophrenia.
sections.black_box: Thioridazine prolongs the QTc interval in a dose-related manner and has been associated with torsades de pointes–type arrhythmias and sudden death. Reserve use for schizophrenia only when other antipsychotics have failed due to inadequate effectiveness or intolerable adverse effects. Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death; thioridazine is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.
other: Do not start if baseline QTc >450 msec
If QTc >500 msec during treatment, discontinue thioridazine
If QTc increases >60 msec from baseline, reassess urgently (dose reduction or switch is typically considered)
Avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs and with CYP2D6 inhibitors (risk of higher levels and greater QTc effect)
Orthostatic hypotension and sedation can increase fall risk
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and tardive dyskinesia can occur, especially with higher doses and longer use
Rare but serious: neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), seizures (lowered threshold), and blood dyscrasias (including agranulocytosis)
patient_counseling: This medication is reserved for specific situations because of heart rhythm risk. You’re not being “over-monitored”—the monitoring is the point.
Tell your clinician immediately about dizziness, fainting, palpitations, chest fluttering, or episodes of near-blackout.
Do not add new prescriptions, OTC meds, or supplements without checking interactions—QT risk can stack fast.
Stand up slowly, hydrate, and watch for lightheadedness—especially during titration.
Report severe stiffness, high fever, confusion, or autonomic symptoms urgently (possible NMS).
If you notice abnormal movements (lip smacking, tongue movements, restlessness), speak up early—don’t wait months.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Common themes: sedation, anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision), orthostatic hypotension, and movement symptoms. Serious risks include QTc prolongation/torsades, blood dyscrasias, tardive dyskinesia, seizures, and NMS.
plain_language_list: Weight gain and sexual side effects can happen
Rare but serious: dangerous heart rhythm changes (QTc prolongation), severe low white blood cells, seizures, NMS

common.patient_note: This can feel like calming at first, but it can also feel like brain fog or heavy fatigue. If you’re too sedated, the dose may be too high or the timing may need adjustment.

common.symptom: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, urinary retention)
common.patient_note: Thioridazine can be particularly “drying” compared to many antipsychotics. Constipation isn’t just uncomfortable—it can become dangerous if ignored. Treat it early and proactively.
Lightheadedness when standing is common during titration. It can raise fall risk, especially if you’re older or on other blood-pressure-lowering medications.
Stiffness, tremor, slowed movements, or restlessness can happen. Dose, individual sensitivity, and other meds all matter.
Some people gain weight and some develop symptoms tied to higher prolactin (menstrual changes, sexual side effects, galactorrhea). If symptoms show up, it’s worth checking and adjusting the plan.

serious: QTc prolongation, torsades de pointes, and sudden death: risk increases with higher doses, bradycardia, low potassium/magnesium, congenital long QT, CYP2D6 inhibition, and other QT-prolonging drugs
Blood dyscrasias (leukopenia, neutropenia, agranulocytosis): can be life-threatening; discontinue if ANC <1,000/mm3
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability—medical emergency
Tardive dyskinesia: potentially irreversible abnormal movements; risk increases with duration and cumulative exposure
Seizures: first-generation antipsychotics can lower seizure threshold
Ocular toxicity at higher doses: pigmentary retinopathy/corneal changes; risk increases above recommended dosing and with higher daily doses

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Thioridazine has a dangerous interaction profile because it can prolong QTc and because CYP2D6 metabolism matters a lot. The safest approach is: treat this medication like it’s “interaction-prone” by default.

items.risk: Additive QTc prolongation increases risk of torsades de pointes and sudden death.
items.action: Avoid combinations whenever possible. If unavoidable, use specialist oversight, baseline + follow-up ECGs, and correct electrolytes.

items.risk: Raises thioridazine levels and can substantially increase QTc risk.
items.action: Avoid. If antidepressant treatment is needed, choose alternatives that do not strongly inhibit CYP2D6 and reassess the antipsychotic plan.

items.risk: Can increase levels and QTc risk (and is specifically listed among combinations to avoid).
Combination is listed as a contraindicated/avoid interaction due to cardiac risk and potential pharmacokinetic effects.
items.action: Avoid. If a beta-blocker is needed, coordinate with cardiology/psychiatry for a safer alternative.

items.with: Electrolyte-lowering agents (anything that can contribute to hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia)
items.risk: Low potassium or magnesium amplifies torsades risk in QT-prolonging medications.
items.action: Monitor electrolytes and correct aggressively if thioridazine is used.

items.with: Other CNS depressants (sedatives, alcohol, some sleep meds)
items.risk: More sedation, more falls, more confusion; can worsen safety and functioning.
items.action: Use caution and simplify the regimen. Avoid stacking sedation when possible.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: For chronic psychotic disorders, clinicians usually switch antipsychotics rather than stopping with no replacement, because relapse risk can be high. If thioridazine is being stopped for tolerability or lack of benefit, a gradual taper over weeks to months is typically used to reduce withdrawal symptoms and to catch early relapse signs. If discontinuation is due to a serious adverse effect (like QTc >500 msec or dangerous blood count changes), the plan may need to be faster and medically supervised.
key_points: If stopping for non-emergency reasons, taper gradually over several weeks to months to reduce withdrawal symptoms and monitor for relapse
Withdrawal symptoms can include agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, GI symptoms, restlessness, tremor, dyskinesias, and rebound psychosis
For switching antipsychotics, common strategies include cross-titration or overlap, tailored to relapse risk and side effect burden
If schizophrenia relapse risk is high, clinicians may maintain the current antipsychotic while the new one is brought to a therapeutic dose, then taper the first over 1-2 weeks (or slower if needed)
Always monitor closely for early warning signs: sleep disruption, rising suspiciousness, social withdrawal, increasing disorganization, or escalating agitation

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Thioridazine dosing is individualized and typically managed by psychiatry because of QTc risk and side effects. The goal is the lowest effective dose, slow titration, and routine safety monitoring (especially ECGs and interacting medications).

adult.schizophrenia_titration: Increase total daily dose by 100-150 mg every 3-4 days based on response and tolerability; monitor sedation, anticholinergic effects, and orthostatic hypotension during titration
adult.schizophrenia_usual: 200-600 mg/day PO in 1-3 divided doses; use the lowest effective maintenance dose
adult.schizophrenia_max: 800 mg/day PO (higher doses increase adverse effect risk, including ocular toxicity and QTc issues)

sections.simple_explanation: This is an older antipsychotic that’s usually dosed multiple times per day. Titration is gradual to balance symptom control with side effects and cardiac safety. The biggest practical rule is: don’t chase higher doses without a clear benefit—risk rises with dose, especially for QTc prolongation.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Pregnancy planning and treatment during pregnancy should be shared decision-making: weigh relapse risk against medication risks, aim for the lowest effective dose, and avoid unnecessary polypharmacy. Thioridazine-specific breastfeeding data are limited. In older adults, antipsychotics carry higher risks (stroke, cognitive decline, falls, mortality in dementia-related psychosis), and thioridazine is generally avoided for dementia behaviors.
sections.pregnancy: Class-level data for first-generation antipsychotics do not show a clear large increase in major congenital malformations overall, but data for individual agents and specific outcomes are limited. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics can cause newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, abnormal tone, feeding problems, respiratory distress, sleepiness, tremor). Do not taper late in pregnancy solely to prevent newborn symptoms; instead, focus on stable psychiatric control. Use the lowest effective dose of a single agent when possible, and reassess risks/benefits continuously.
sections.lactation: It is not known if thioridazine is present in human milk. If breastfeeding is planned or ongoing, coordinate with psychiatry and pediatrics to choose the safest effective option and to monitor the infant for sedation, feeding difficulty, poor weight gain, or abnormal movements.
sections.pediatrics: Not commonly used today in children and adolescents because safer and better-tolerated options (often second-generation antipsychotics) are typically preferred. If used in refractory cases, dosing is weight-based and requires careful monitoring for dystonia/EPS, prolactin-related effects, and overall tolerability. Gradual tapering is recommended if discontinuing to reduce withdrawal symptoms and relapse risk.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid for behavioral problems associated with dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic options have failed and there is risk of harm. Antipsychotics in older adults carry higher risks (falls, orthostatic hypotension, cognitive effects), and antipsychotics increase mortality risk in dementia-related psychosis. If used for schizophrenia in late-onset cases, lower-range adult doses are often sufficient; titrate slowly and monitor carefully.
sections.hepatic: No formal manufacturer dose adjustment is provided, but use caution because metabolism is hepatic and accumulation can occur. Start low, titrate slowly, and monitor sedation, orthostasis, and adverse effects.
sections.renal: No dosage adjustments are provided in manufacturer labeling; monitor clinically and keep an eye on overall medication burden and hydration/electrolytes.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: ECG (QTc): Baseline before starting; avoid initiation if QTc >450 ms. Recheck after significant dose increases, when adding any QT-prolonging medication, or if symptoms suggest arrhythmia (dizziness, palpitations, syncope). Discontinue if QTc >500 ms.
Electrolytes (especially potassium and magnesium): Check baseline and as clinically indicated; correct abnormalities promptly because low K/Mg increases torsades risk.
Vital signs and orthostatics: Monitor for hypotension and fall risk, especially during titration and in older adults.
Mental status and functioning: Every visit—track hallucinations, delusions, disorganization, agitation, sleep, and real-world functioning (work, school, relationships).
Movement symptoms (EPS): Every visit early on; use a structured scale periodically. Reassess after dose changes and at least annually (more often if high risk).
Tardive dyskinesia: Screen regularly; use a formal scale at least annually (or every 6 months if high risk).

CBC: As clinically indicated, especially if there’s a history of low WBC or prior drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia; discontinue for severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis concerns (including ANC <1,000/mm3).

Metabolic monitoring: Weight/BMI frequently early on (every visit for first 6 months, then quarterly). Consider fasting glucose/HbA1c and lipid panel around 4 months after initiation and then annually (or more often if abnormal).
Prolactin-related symptoms: Ask about menstrual changes, libido changes, galactorrhea, gynecomastia, erectile/ejaculatory issues; check levels if symptomatic.
Ocular monitoring: Consider periodic eye exams, especially at higher daily doses (e.g., ≥600 mg/day) or if visual symptoms develop, due to risk of pigmentary/retinal changes with higher exposure.
Fall risk: Evaluate regularly in older adults and anyone reporting dizziness, sedation, or unsteadiness.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Thioridazine is available as an oral tablet in multiple strengths, usually taken in divided doses.
items: Oral tablets (thioridazine HCl): 10 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Thioridazine is a first-generation antipsychotic that primarily blocks dopamine receptors (especially D2) in brain pathways involved in psychosis. It also affects other receptor systems (including histamine and cholinergic pathways), which helps explain why it can feel sedating and why it can cause anticholinergic side effects like dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, and urinary retention.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Thioridazine sits in a very narrow lane: refractory schizophrenia when other antipsychotics haven’t worked or weren’t tolerable. The deciding factor isn’t convenience—it’s safety. Because QTc prolongation risk is dose-related and potentially life-threatening, clinicians generally prefer other antipsychotics first. If thioridazine is used, it’s usually with specialist oversight, careful ECG monitoring, strict interaction avoidance, and a constant push toward the lowest effective dose.

seo.title: Thioridazine (Mellaril): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects, QTc Warning
seo.description: Thioridazine (Mellaril) is a last-line antipsychotic for schizophrenia due to dose-related QTc prolongation and torsades risk. Learn dosing, side effects, interactions, monitoring, and safe discontinuation.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Thioridazine is reserved for schizophrenia when other antipsychotics haven’t worked well enough or weren’t tolerable. It’s not a first- or second-line medication because it can dangerously prolong the QTc interval and has been linked to torsades de pointes and sudden death.

faqs.q: Why is thioridazine considered a “last-line” antipsychotic?
faqs.a: Because the cardiac risk is real and dose-related. Thioridazine can prolong QTc, which can trigger a rare but deadly rhythm called torsades de pointes. That’s why it’s generally used only after adequate trials of other antipsychotics.

faqs.q: Do I need an ECG if I’m taking thioridazine?
faqs.a: Yes—ECG monitoring is a core part of safe use. It’s typically checked before starting, after meaningful dose increases, and when adding any medication that can affect QTc or thioridazine levels. If QTc is >500 ms, thioridazine is usually discontinued.

faqs.q: How is thioridazine dosed for schizophrenia?
faqs.a: A common starting range is 50-100 mg taken three times daily. The dose may be increased in steps (often 100-150 mg/day every 3-4 days) based on response and tolerability. Usual total daily dosing is often 200-600 mg/day, and the maximum is typically 800 mg/day.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects people notice?
faqs.a: Sleepiness, dizziness when standing, dry mouth, constipation, and blurry vision are common. Movement side effects (stiffness, tremor, restlessness) can also occur. If sedation or constipation is significant, that’s a signal to adjust the plan.

faqs.q: Can thioridazine help with agitation or insomnia?
faqs.a: It can feel calming and sedating, which may reduce agitation and make sleep easier for some people. But it’s not prescribed primarily as a sleep medication, and the QTc risk means it shouldn’t be used casually for sedation.

faqs.q: Which drug interactions matter the most with thioridazine?
faqs.a: The biggest concerns are: (1) other QT-prolonging medications (risk stacks), and (2) CYP2D6 inhibitors like fluoxetine or paroxetine, which can raise thioridazine levels and increase QTc risk. Always check interactions before starting anything new.

faqs.q: Is thioridazine safe in older adults with dementia-related psychosis?
faqs.a: No—thioridazine is not approved for dementia-related psychosis. Antipsychotics in general increase mortality risk in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis, and thioridazine adds extra cardiac safety concerns.

faqs.q: How do I stop thioridazine safely?
faqs.a: If it’s not an emergency, it’s usually tapered gradually over weeks to months to reduce withdrawal symptoms and to watch for early relapse. In chronic psychotic disorders, clinicians often switch to another antipsychotic rather than stopping without a replacement.

faqs.q: What symptoms should make me seek urgent care while on thioridazine?
faqs.a: Fainting, near-fainting, new palpitations, chest fluttering, severe dizziness, or episodes of sudden weakness can be warning signs of a rhythm problem—get urgent evaluation. Also seek urgent care for high fever with stiffness/confusion (possible NMS) or signs of severe infection if blood counts are a concern.

faqs.q: What’s the bottom line on thioridazine?
faqs.a: It can help schizophrenia, but it’s a high-monitoring, high-caution medication. If it’s part of your plan, the goal is tight safety screening, careful ECG monitoring, avoiding risky interactions, and using the lowest dose that actually helps.
